title: Omen AI Acquires Aquatic Labs for $16M in Water Tech Deal
summary: Omen AI acquires Aquatic Labs for $16 million to combine real-time water monitoring technologies for data center cooling systems in November 2026.
body_markdown:
#### 💡 TL;DR


- Omen AI acquired Aquatic Labs for $16 million in cash and stock to combine complementary real-time water monitoring technologies.
- The merged sensor platform will monitor both water composition and alkalinity, targeting data centers that use 17-19 billion gallons annually.
- Integrated sensors expected to launch early 2027, monitoring 250-300 MW of chip power by end of 2026.


Omen AI has acquired competitor Aquatic Labs in a $16 million cash-and-stock transaction, combining two real-time water monitoring platforms to address the escalating water demands of AI data centers. Officially launched on November 2, 2026, the deal unites complementary sensor technologies that promise to reduce water waste and improve cooling system efficiency across the rapidly expanding AI infrastructure sector.


## Why Data Centers Need Better Water Monitoring


US data centers consume between 17 and 19 billion gallons of water annually to cool high-performance chips, a figure expected to triple within five years according to the Water Foundation. Traditional monitoring requires sending fluid samples to external laboratories, a multi-day process that leaves operators blind to real-time system health. When cooling systems fail or bacterial growth threatens water flow, data center managers typically dump contaminated fluid and shut down operations rather than risk damaging expensive hardware.


Omen AI, founded in 2024, developed sensors that detect elemental composition in cooling fluids. Aquatic Labs built complementary technology focused on alkalinity testing. The combined sensor platform creates what chief science officer Allan Adams describes as a "much richer picture of the water and the fluid," enabling operators to extend fluid lifecycles and prevent costly emergency shutdowns.


## Complementary Founder DNA


The acquisition bridges two distinct entrepreneurial backgrounds. Omen founder Zach Laberge dropped out of high school to launch his first company analyzing hydraulic fluids for construction equipment. Adams, a physicist by training, spent his academic career at MIT and Woods Hole Oceanographic Institute developing advanced ocean sensing technology before transitioning to commercial applications. An investor in the filtration space introduced the two CEOs, recognizing the strategic fit between their technologies.


With Adams now serving as chief science officer, the combined teams are integrating both sensor capabilities into a unified platform expected to reach market in early 2027. The merged technology automates what had been a slow, manual laboratory process, delivering real-time visibility into cooling system health.


## Current Deployment and Growth Targets


Omen's initial sensors will monitor chips pulling 250 to 300 megawatts of power by the end of 2026, representing approximately $5 to $7 billion in hardware value. The company aims to scale to 1 gigawatt of monitored chip capacity by the end of 2027. Real-time monitoring enables operators to maximize fluid reuse while minimizing downtime, translating directly to operational cost savings.


Beyond data centers, Adams sees broader environmental applications. "Water goes into data centers, and then it comes out and gets dumped into municipal water, and you want that whole process to happen in a way that's as safe and responsible as possible, and that means you got to measure stuff," he told TechCrunch.


## Market Resilience Amid Infrastructure Skepticism


Despite recent skepticism around AI infrastructure spending that sent hyperscaler stocks tumbling, Omen remains confident in its market position. The company serves existing and near-term data center builds rather than speculative future projects. "We're working customers on stuff they're building today or have already built, and so it doesn't really affect us because all of those projects were financed 12 months ago," Laberge explained. Even if projected AI infrastructure spending falls short of the estimated $4 trillion by 2030, Laberge maintains the market "is still going to be the biggest market in human history, even if you sliced it in half."


## What This Means


The Omen AI and Aquatic Labs merger consolidates real-time fluid monitoring expertise at a critical inflection point for data center sustainability. As AI workloads drive unprecedented water consumption, sensor technologies that extend cooling system lifecycles and prevent costly shutdowns become infrastructure essentials rather than optional upgrades. The combined platform positions the merged entity to capture growing demand for operational efficiency tools that reduce both environmental impact and downtime costs across the expanding AI hardware landscape.
